# Tobit Chapter 4 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** That same day, Tobit suddenly remembered the money he had left in trust with Gabael over in Rages of Media.

**2** He thought to himself, "I've been praying to die — so why haven't I called Tobias and told him about that money while I still can?"

**3** He called his son and said to him: "When I'm gone, bury me properly, and don't neglect your mother. Treat her with honor as long as she lives. Do what makes her happy, and never give her cause for grief.

**4** Think about everything she went through carrying you in her womb, my son — all the danger she faced for your sake. When she dies, lay her to rest beside me in the same grave.

**5** Every single day of your life, keep God in your thoughts, and make up your mind never to sin or break his commands. Live righteously all your days, and stay off the roads that lead nowhere good.

**6** If you live honestly, everything you do will turn out well — that's true for everyone who does what's right.

**7** Give generously to those in need, and don't let a mean spirit hold your hand back. Never look away from someone who is poor, and God will never look away from you.

**8** Give what you can afford. If you have a lot, be generous. If you have very little, don't be afraid to give from even that.

**9** Every act of generosity is a treasure you are laying up for yourself — savings you'll draw on when hard times come.

**10** Generosity saves people from death and keeps them out of the darkness.

**11** There is no greater offering before God Most High than a merciful, generous heart.

**12** Stay far away from sexual immorality, my son. And when it comes time to marry, find your wife among our own people — don't marry outside our tribe. We are children of the prophets. Think about Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, our ancient fathers. Every one of them married from within their own family, and they were blessed in their children, and their descendants will inherit the land.

**13** So love your people, son. Don't let pride make you look down on your brothers and sisters or treat them as beneath you when you choose a wife. Pride leads to disaster and chaos; laziness leads to poverty and hunger — idleness is the mother of famine.

**14** Never hold back a worker's wages past sundown — pay people what they've earned, right away. Live in God's service and you'll be repaid yourself. Be careful in everything you do, and hold yourself to a high standard in how you live.

**15** The rule is simple: don't do to others what you yourself would hate. Don't drink too much wine, and don't let drunkenness tag along with you on the road.

**16** Share your food with the hungry. Give clothing to those who have none. Whatever you have in abundance, give some away — and don't let a stingy eye stop you.

**17** Lay bread at the graves of the righteous, but don't share your food with people who live wickedly.

**18** Ask advice from wise people, and take good counsel seriously wherever you find it.

**19** Bless the Lord your God at every turn, and ask him to straighten your path and make your plans succeed. Because no nation figures things out on its own — God himself gives every good gift. He lifts up and humbles people exactly as he sees fit. So now, son, keep what I've told you in your heart — don't let it slip away.

**20** And there's something practical I need to tell you: I left ten silver talents in trust with Gabael son of Gabrias at Rages in Media.

**21** Don't let our poverty frighten you, son. You are rich in what matters — if you fear God, turn your back on every sin, and do what is right before the Lord your God.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

- **Generosity as a theme** (vv. 7–11, 16–17): The Greek *eleēmosynē* is rendered contextually as "generosity," "giving," and "merciful, generous heart" — the term carries legal, relational, and devotional weight that "alms" alone doesn't convey to modern readers. The through-line is covenant faithfulness expressed through material sharing.
- **v. 15 — The negative Golden Rule**: "Don't do to others what you yourself would hate" is rendered in plain modern idiom while staying true to the Greek. This is one of the oldest recorded statements of this principle; its directness should land with full force.
- **v. 3 "When I'm gone"**: The Greek says "when I die" — PNEUMA softens slightly for natural speech rhythm without losing the reality of death.
- **v. 17 "lay bread at graves"**: The original practice of placing food at gravesites of righteous people is retained; no attempt to explain or sanitize this ancient custom.
- **v. 12 — Endogamy command**: The instruction to marry within the tribe is rendered in its social reality. The list of patriarchs is kept because it functions as an appeal to ancestral authority, which is emotionally important in the narrative.
- **v. 20**: The shift to "there's something practical I need to tell you" signals the transition from ethical testament to plot mechanics — the money in Rages is what drives the entire story forward. — PNEUMA
